title: Review 2: Fabric weight and warp preparation

quizzes.title: Key terms across the lectures
quizzes.intro: The terms of fabric weight and warp preparation.

questions.q: In the construction 20 × 16 / 128 × 60, 63", the number 128 is
questions.explain: The construction reads warp count × weft count / ends per inch × picks per inch, width.

questions.q: GSM stands for
options: Grams per standard metre of yarn
questions.explain: It is the weight in grams of one square metre of fabric.

questions.q: A warper’s beam carries
options: All the ends of the fabric, sized
Part of the ends, unsized, from one creel
questions.explain: Several warper’s beams are combined on the sizing machine into one weaver’s beam.

questions.q: The creel of a warping machine is
options: The frame holding the cones that feed it
The drum that drives the beam
The comb that spaces the ends
questions.explain: One cone on the creel feeds one end on the beam, so creel capacity limits the ends per beam.

questions.q: Size add-on is
options: The extra length gained in sizing
The weight of size added, as a percentage of yarn weight
The speed of the sizing machine
questions.explain: Size adds weight but no length, so the sized yarn behaves like a coarser count.

questions.q: Packing density of a beam is quoted in the lecture as
questions.explain: About 56 in³ per lb for a warper’s beam and 60 for a sized beam.

questions.q: Breaks per 10 million metres lets warps of different counts be compared fairly.
questions.explain: A pound of fine yarn is much longer than a pound of coarse yarn, so breaks must be related to length, not weight.

questions.q: Warp contraction means that
options: The warp yarn in a length of fabric is longer than the fabric
The fabric is narrower than the reed
questions.explain: The ends bend over the picks, so extra warp length is needed for each metre of cloth.

questions.q: A “set” of warper’s beams is always an even number in the lecture because
options: Even numbers are easier to count
Beams are loaded in pairs on the sizing creel
questions.explain: The sizing creel takes beams in pairs, so the number is rounded up to the next even figure.

questions.q: The same beam holds a greater length when it carries fewer ends.
questions.explain: The weight on the beam is fixed by its volume, and length = weight × 840 × Ne ÷ ends.

quizzes.title: Linking the ideas
quizzes.intro: How one quantity changes another in preparation.

questions.q: If the picks per inch of a fabric are increased, its weight per square metre
questions.explain: More picks mean more weft yarn in every metre.

questions.q: If a finer warp count is used with the same ends per inch, the warp weight per yard
questions.explain: Warp weight = ends × (1 + contraction) ÷ (840 × Ne), so a higher Ne gives less weight.

questions.q: Total ends are 8,104 and the creel holds 840 cones. The beams needed are
questions.explain: 8,104 ÷ 840 = 9.65, rounded up to the next even number: 10 beams.

questions.q: The volume of yarn on a beam is
questions.explain: It is the full cylinder less the barrel: a hollow cylinder of yarn.

questions.q: A warp of Ne 20 takes 12.5% size add-on. Its sized count is
questions.explain: Sized count = 20 ÷ 1.125 = 17.8: heavier per unit length, so a lower count.

questions.q: For the same weight per break, a finer yarn has
options: The same breaks per 10 million metres
questions.explain: A pound of fine yarn is longer, so one break per so many pounds is spread over more metres.

questions.q: A sized beam of the same dimensions holds slightly less weight than a warper’s beam, because sized yarn packs less densely.
questions.explain: 60 in³ per lb against 56 in³ per lb: the size film makes the yarn bulkier.

questions.q: For a short sample warp, a full-size cone is wasteful because
options: It cannot fit on the creel
Only a little yarn is needed from each cone and the rest is left over
questions.explain: The sample needs only a short length per end, so small cones of just that length are wound.

questions.q: The yards warped per shift are found from
questions.explain: Every turn of the drum winds one circumference; multiply by turns and by the share of time actually run.

questions.q: The quick rule GSM ≈ (EPI ÷ Ne warp + PPI ÷ Ne weft) × 25 includes the exact contraction and width of the fabric.
questions.explain: It assumes typical contraction and ignores width, so it is only a first estimate.

quizzes.title: Mixed calculations
quizzes.intro: Weight, beams and capacity to calculate.

questions.q: A fabric has 72 ends per inch and is 60 inches wide. How many ends are in the warp (ignore selvedges)?
Use the quick rule to estimate the GSM of 20 × 20 / 60 × 60.
A warp has 4,200 ends of Ne 20 with 10% contraction. What is the warp weight per yard of fabric in lb, to three decimals?
A fabric has 60 picks per inch of Ne 20 weft, is 63 inches (1.75 yd) wide, and weft contraction is 5%. What is the weft weight per yard of fabric in lb, to four decimals?
questions.explain: Picks per yard 2,160 × pick length 1.8375 yd ÷ 16,800 = 0.2362 lb.

questions.q: A warp has 5,000 ends including selvedge and the creel holds 840 cones. How many warper’s beams are used (rounded up to an even number)?
questions.explain: 5,000 ÷ 840 = 5.95, rounded up to the next even number: 6 beams.

questions.q: A beam has a full diameter of 30 in, a barrel of 10 in and 60 in between flanges. What is the volume of yarn in cubic inches, to the nearest whole number?
A warper’s beam holds 800 lb of Ne 20 yarn in 640 ends. What length of warp is on the beam, in yards?
A warp of Ne 30 breaks once every 40 lb. How many yards are warped per break?
A warping drum of 30 inch diameter turns at 300 rpm. How many yards does it wind in an hour at 100% efficiency, to the nearest yard?
questions.explain: Circumference 94.25 in × 18,000 turns ÷ 36 = 47,124 yards.

questions.q: A shed of 150 looms each weaves 400 m a day. Warp contraction is 10%. How many metres of sized warp are needed per day?
questions.explain: 60,000 m of fabric × 1.10 = 66,000 metres of warp.

quizzes.title: Case study
quizzes.intro: One order followed from its construction to the warper’s time.

questions.q: How many ends are in the warp, including the selvedge ends?
questions.explain: 76 × 63 = 4,788, plus 40 selvedge ends = 4,828.

questions.q: How many warper’s beams are needed (rounded up to an even number)?
questions.explain: 4,828 ÷ 840 = 5.75, rounded up to the next even number: 6.

questions.q: How many ends go on each beam on average, to one decimal?
questions.explain: 4,828 ÷ 6 = 804.7 ends per beam.

questions.q: What is the warp weight per yard of fabric in lb, to four decimals?
What is the weft weight per yard of fabric in lb, to four decimals?
questions.explain: 2,448 picks per yard × 1.8375 yd per pick ÷ 25,200 = 0.1785 lb.

questions.q: How many yards of fabric is the order, to the nearest yard? (1 m = 1.0936 yd)
What length of warp is required, to the nearest yard?
questions.explain: 32,808 yd of fabric × 1.08 = 35,433 yards of warp.

questions.q: What weight of warp yarn is required, to the nearest lb?
How long does the warper take to make all six beams, in hours to one decimal?
questions.explain: 6 beams × 35,433 yd = 212,596 yd; ÷ 560 yd a minute ÷ 60 = 6.3 hours.

questions.q: If the creel held 1,024 cones instead of 840, the order would need
questions.explain: 4,828 ÷ 1,024 = 4.71, which still rounds up to the next even number, 6.

quizzes.case: An order is for 30,000 metres of 30 × 30 / 76 × 68, 63 inches wide. Warp contraction is 8% and weft contraction 5%. There are 40 extra selvedge ends. The warper’s creel holds 840 cones, and the warper runs at 800 yards a minute at 70% efficiency.

questions.q: Fabric: 20 × 20 / 60 × 60, 63 in wide; warp contraction 10%, weft 5%. Warp weighs 0.2475 lb and weft 0.2363 lb per linear yard. What is the weight in ounces per square yard, to two decimals?
questions.explain: 0.4838 lb × 16 = 7.74 oz per linear yard; ÷ 1.75 yd width = 4.42 oz per square yard.

questions.q: A beam has full diameter 36 in, barrel 18 in and 66 in between flanges. With a packing density of 56 in³ per lb, what weight of yarn does it hold, to the nearest lb?
A sized beam holds 840 lb of sized Ne 20 warp with 12.5% add-on, in 3,820 ends. What length of warp is on it, to the nearest yard?
A warp of Ne 60 breaks once every 27 lb. How many breaks is that per 10 million metres, to one decimal? (1 m = 1.0936 yd)
100 bags of 100 lb are in store, wound in cones of 4.17 lb. A creel needs 640 cones. How many complete creels can be filled?
questions.explain: 10,000 lb ÷ 4.17 = 2,398 cones; ÷ 640 = 3.7, so 3 complete creels.

questions.q: A sample warp of 396 m is needed on each of 6 beams from the same cones, in Ne 20. Taking 15,362 m of Ne 20 per lb, what cone weight is needed in lb, to three decimals?
questions.explain: Each cone feeds 6 beams: 396 × 6 = 2,376 m; ÷ 15,362 m per lb = 0.155 lb.

questions.q: One sizing machine can size 108,000 m a day. A shed needs 110,000 m of sized warp a day for each 200 looms. How many sizing machines are needed for 600 looms, to two decimals?
questions.explain: 330,000 ÷ 108,000 = 3.06, so four machines in practice.

questions.q: Two mills report warp breaks: mill X one break per 51 lb on Ne 21, mill Y one break per 44 lb on Ne 30. Which has the better (lower) break rate per unit length?
questions.explain: Yards per break: X = 21 × 51 × 840 = 899,640; Y = 30 × 44 × 840 = 1,108,800. Y runs longer between breaks.

questions.q: A beam of 3,820 sized ends holds far less length than a warper’s beam of 637 ends of the same yarn and size.
questions.explain: Roughly six times as many ends share about the same weight, so the length is about one sixth.

questions.q: The looms of a shed are speeded up so that each weaves 10% more fabric a day. The sized warp needed per day
questions.explain: Warp consumption follows fabric production, so warping and sizing must supply 10% more length.
